title: Swartland
description: A dry, rugged land north of Cape Town where old bush vines sparked a South African wine revolution.
L: Swartland, black land, lies about 65 km north of Cape Town, named after the dark renosterbos shrub that covers its hills. It's a large area of wheat fields and vineyards, around towns like Malmesbury and Riebeek-Kasteel, with the Paardeberg and Kasteelberg mountains. Soils include granite, schist and iron-rich clay.

Swartland is warmer and drier than Stellenbosch, with hot summers and about 300 to 600 mm of rain a year, mostly in winter. Many vines are bush vines, dry-farmed without irrigation, their deep roots finding water. That keeps yields low and fruit concentrated. Atlantic breezes cool some western areas.
Dry-farmed bush vines in a hot, dry climate
Without irrigation, old vines give small crops.

In the early 2000s, winemakers like Eben Sadie and Adi Badenhorst, then Chris and Andrea Mullineux, came to Swartland, drawn by old, forgotten vineyards. They made natural, low-intervention wines from old Chenin, Syrah and Grenache. In 2010, the Swartland Independent Producers set rules: no added yeast, no acidification, minimal sulphur, no new oak.
Swartland's revival was led by young producers using old vineyards.
Swartland, the black land, lies north of Cape Town
It's hot and dry, with dry-farmed bush vines
A wave of young producers revived it from the 2000s

Swartland is famous for old-vine Chenin Blanc, from dry-farmed bush vines, some over 50 years old. The wines are concentrated, textured and mineral, with quince, stone fruit, honey and fresh acidity, often fermented in old barrels or concrete. Chenin is often blended with other white grapes, like Grenache Blanc, Clairette, Roussanne and Viognier, in Cape white blends.

Rhône grapes suit the heat and drought: Syrah gives peppery, savoury reds; Grenache gives red fruit and spice; Cinsault, light, fresh reds; Mourvèdre and Carignan add structure. Blends of these, inspired by the Rhône, are a Swartland signature. Sadie Family's Columella is a famous Syrah-led blend.

Reading Swartland and eating with it

Labels show Wine of Origin Swartland, the producer, the grape or blend and sometimes a ward, like Paardeberg or Riebeekberg. The Certified Heritage Vineyards seal marks vines over 35 years old. The Swartland Independent seal marks minimal-intervention wines. Many producers are small.
Wine of Origin, heritage and independent seals

Old-vine Chenin suits roast chicken, pork, seafood, Cape Malay curries and bobotie. Syrah and Rhône blends suit lamb, game, the braai and mushroom dishes. Light Cinsault suits charcuterie and can be served slightly cool. Serve Chenin at 10 to 12 degrees, reds at 15 to 17.
